blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Coaching a senior executive is a very different discipline from coaching a new manager. The brief is rarely about skills. Almost always, it is about the hidden patterns — how the executive reacts under pressure, which feedback they fail to hear, and where their strengths have started to harden into liabilities.

A good executive coach earns the right to challenge through patient listening. They do not rush to diagnose, and they are comfortable sitting with an uncomfortable silence. Often they recommend that the coachee spend more time where they are least comfortable, rather than where they are most naturally skilled.

Feedback at senior level requires equal care. The common mistake is either to soften it into uselessness, or to deliver it with an edge that invites defensiveness. The best feedback pairs a specific observation with a genuinely open invitation to reflect. It is essential that the conversation leave the executive with a question they want to sit with, not a verdict they need to defend.

items.q: According to the text, what is executive coaching usually about?
options: The technical skills the executive still lacks
The performance of the executive's direct reports
The hidden patterns in how the executive behaves
items.why: "Almost always, it is about the hidden patterns" — não sobre habilidades.

items.q: How does a good coach earn the right to challenge?
items.why: "A good executive coach earns the right to challenge through patient listening."

items.q: The best feedback, according to the text, should leave the executive with…
options: a verdict they need to defend
a question they want to sit with
items.why: "a question they want to sit with, not a verdict they need to defend."

items.q: Which statement would the author most likely DISAGREE with?
options: Silence can be a productive part of a coaching conversation
Coaching a senior leader differs from coaching a new manager
A strength can eventually become a weakness
Softening feedback until it is harmless is the safest approach
items.why: Inferência: o texto diz que suavizar até a inutilidade é tão prejudicial quanto entregar com aspereza.

items.q: The phrase "where their strengths have started to harden into liabilities" suggests that…
options: an overused strength can turn into a weakness
senior executives rarely have real strengths
strengths should always be reinforced further
items.why: Inferência: uma força levada longe demais e sem consciência vira passivo — daí "harden into liabilities".

blocks.instruction: Ouça Emily conduzindo uma sessão de coaching com um líder sênior. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
So, before we talk about the team, I'd like to stay with something you said a moment ago. You mentioned that people have gone quiet in your meetings — and then you moved on rather quickly. I'd like us to sit with that for a second.

Here's what I've noticed across our sessions. When a decision feels urgent, you become sharper, faster, more certain. That is a genuine strength — it's part of why you're where you are. But I wonder whether, under pressure, that same edge is landing on the room as impatience. People stop offering half-formed ideas, because half-formed ideas don't survive contact with you.

I'm not asking you to soften who you are. What I'd suggest is an experiment. In your next three meetings, when you feel the urge to close a point, hold it. Count to five. Ask one more question before you decide.

And notice how the room responds. I'm not handing you a verdict here — I'm handing you a question. Where might your certainty be costing you the very engagement you're worried about?
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What does Emily choose to focus on at the start of the session?
options: Something the executive said and then moved past quickly
A complaint filed by a direct report
items.why: "You mentioned that people have gone quiet… and then you moved on rather quickly. I'd like us to sit with that."

items.q: What strength does Emily identify in the executive?
options: Becoming sharper and more certain when a decision feels urgent
items.why: "When a decision feels urgent, you become sharper, faster, more certain. That is a genuine strength."

items.q: What experiment does Emily propose?
options: Holding a point and asking one more question before deciding
Writing feedback down instead of speaking it
Delegating all decisions to the team
items.why: "when you feel the urge to close a point, hold it… Ask one more question before you decide."

items.q: What does Emily imply about the team going quiet?
options: The executive's own impatience may be silencing them
The team is disengaged for reasons outside the executive's control
The meetings are scheduled too often
The team lacks the skills to contribute
items.why: Inferência: "half-formed ideas don't survive contact with you" — o próprio comportamento do líder cala a sala.

items.q: How would you best describe Emily's coaching approach here?
options: She delivers a firm verdict and expects compliance
She avoids the difficult point to protect the relationship
She names a strength, then invites the executive to reflect through a question
She recommends the executive change their personality entirely
items.why: Inferência: "I'm not handing you a verdict… I'm handing you a question" — observação + convite à reflexão.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "Her decisiveness, once an asset, had quietly become a liability." A liability is…
items.why: Liability = passivo/fraqueza: aquilo que joga contra você.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "A coach must first ___ the right to challenge before offering any hard truths."
items.why: To earn the right = conquistar o direito, pela escuta paciente antes de desafiar.

items.q: "He couldn't see it himself — it was a genuine blind spot." A blind spot is…
options: an area a person fails to see about themselves
items.why: Blind spot = ponto cego: algo sobre si que a pessoa não enxerga.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Rather than a rating, she offered an open ___ to reflect on what had happened."
items.why: Invitation to reflect = convite à reflexão, o oposto de um veredicto fechado.

items.q: "Delivered too bluntly, feedback triggers defensiveness instead of insight." Defensiveness is…
options: the reflex to protect oneself against criticism
items.why: Defensiveness = defensividade: o reflexo de se proteger ao ser criticado.

blocks.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em conversas de coaching e feedback executivo. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Give her the space to open up before you offer any advice." To open up means to…
options: become more willing to share honestly
items.why: Open up = abrir-se, passar a compartilhar com franqueza.

items.q: "The executive agreed to the plan but never followed through." They…
options: failed to carry it to completion
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi combinado — aqui, o que faltou.

items.q: "A single question can move the needle on self-awareness more than an hour of advice." This means it can…
items.why: Move the needle = mexer o ponteiro, fazer diferença perceptível.

items.q: "When challenged, he tended to push back before really hearing the point." To push back means to…
items.why: Push back = resistir, contestar — reagir contra antes de escutar.

items.q: "Try not to gloss over the discomfort — that is exactly where the insight lives." To gloss over means to…
options: deal with something too briefly to avoid difficulty
treat something as more important than it is
items.why: Gloss over = passar por cima, tratar superficialmente para evitar o que incomoda.
